newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik president, Islamist opponent agree to talks.
newsitem.headline: Tajik president, Islamist opponent agree to talks.

text.p: The head of Tajikistan's embattled government and his Islamist opponent agreed on Monday to talks next month but few believe the news signals an immediate end to bloodshed in the former Soviet republic.

Tajik president Imomali Rakhmonov will meet opposition leader Sayid Abdullo Nuri on December 9, somewhere in northern Afghanistan, a country where the opposition have had bases during the past four years of civil war.

"It will be a preliminary meeting," Rakhmonov's spokesman Zafar Sayidov told Reuters, saying the talks would prepare the way for an accord to be signed in Moscow on December 23 leading to a power-sharing arrangement.

Yusuf Khakim, an opposition spokesman based in the Tajik capital Dushanbe, confirmed the meeting but gave no further details on the possible accord. Two previous meetings planned this year between Rakhmonov and Nuri never took place.

"There's no alternative to a political solution -- this war could carry on without end as it has done in Afghanistan," said Khakim, who works on a commission observing a U.N.-sponsored ceasefire which is regularly flouted by both sides.
There is growing pressure on both sides from the United Nations and Russia to end the civil war, which has cost upwards of 40,000 lives. Many more have lost their homes.
The U.N. fields military observers in the remote mountainous republic bordering Afghanistan and China and is losing patience.

Russia, which has around 20,000 troops guarding Tajikistan's border and carrying out peace-keeping duties, is also anxious for a settlement. But most in Tajikistan see only an upsurge in fighting from the promised talks.
"In any preparation for negotiations there has always been a recrudesence of military activity as each side tries to consolidate its position," said a seasoned diplomat in Dushanbe.

At the end of last week, unidentified gunmen twice attacked buses carrying Russian soldiers in the Tajik capital, killing three Russian servicemen and wounding a further six. The government blamed the opposition.
"These attacks were simply a way for the opposition to say: 'We're here'," the diplomat said.
Neither is there any end to fighting east of Dushanbe, ringed by snow-capped mountains, between government forces and the Islamist guerrillas.

Opposition fighters, which now control over half the country, are said by aid workers to be only 80 km (50 miles) east of Dushanbe and -- as last week's attacks show -- able to operate with relative impunity inside the capital.
Extra checkpoints have been thrown up around the city and Russian armoured vehicles patrol the streets.
"We've been watching the (Dushanbe) bazaar and we've noticed an increase in young men of fighting age from opposition-held territory," said a Russian officer on condition of anonymity.
"These talks are only going to mean more attacks," said the officer resignedly. "The opposition want to show that the government cannot control Dushanbe."
Rakhmonov's own position appears weaker as popular discontent grows and Russian support wanes. Rumours of an imminent coup swept the republic last July.
"The Russians were about to remove him (in a coup) but held back after the (radical Islamic) Taleban militia advanced northwards in Afghanistan,' said the diplomat.
"They didn't want any internal disorder as the events in Afghanistan unfolded," he said. Russia is keen to halt the northward spread of radical Islam into former Soviet territory.
